z-m-15-01.title: What happens to the mean when one more record is added?
z-m-15-01.topic: Change in the mean (when one more data value is added)
z-m-15-01.goal: Judge first how the mean changes when one more data value is added, then find several values that give a target range for the mean, testing your intuition with numbers.
z-m-15-01.material: A basketball club played 5 games. The points scored in each game were 8, 12, 9, 15, and 11. The points in one game are a whole number (not a decimal or fraction) from 0 to 25. After the 6th game, we find the new '6-game mean score.' (The mean score is defined as the total points divided by the number of games.)
z-m-15-01.thinking.0: Reasoning about how a new value relates to the mean
z-m-15-01.thinking.1: Finding several values that satisfy a condition
z-m-15-01.thinking.2: Using numbers to disprove a wrong intuition
z-m-15-01.prereq.0: Experience knowing what the mean is and finding the mean of simple data (grades 5-6 level)
z-m-15-01.prereq.1: The four arithmetic operations with natural numbers
z-m-15-01.s.s1.prompt: The mean score over the first 5 games is 11 points. If the club scores 12 points in the 6th game (1 point higher than the current mean), what happens to the 6-game mean score?
z-m-15-01.s.s1.hint.0: First check that the mean of the first 5 games really is 11 points.
z-m-15-01.s.s1.hint.1: Suppose the 6th game's score is 12 points, and find the mean of all 6 games directly.
z-m-15-01.s.s1.o.a: It becomes 12 points, so the mean goes up by 1 point
z-m-15-01.s.s1.r.a: You treated the new score as if it becomes the mean. Think about the fact that the scores of the first 5 games are also part of the mean.
z-m-15-01.s.s1.o.b: It becomes higher than 11 points but lower than 12 points
z-m-15-01.s.s1.r.b: This judgment sees that a new score above the mean raises the mean, but because the number of games grows, it does not rise all the way to that score.
z-m-15-01.s.s1.o.c: Only the number of games grows, so it stays 11 points even though the score is higher
z-m-15-01.s.s1.r.c: You thought that adding a game with a score above the mean leaves the mean unchanged. Think about how the total changes.
z-m-15-01.s.s1.o.d: The number of games grows to 6, so it becomes lower than 11 points
z-m-15-01.s.s1.r.d: You looked only at the number of games growing and did not think about the size of the new score. What matters is whether the added score is higher or lower than the mean.
z-m-15-01.s.s1.explain: The total of the first 5 games is 55 points, and adding 12 gives 67 points. 67÷6 is about 11.17 points, which is higher than 11 but short of 12. If the new score is higher than the mean, the mean goes up, but because the number of games grows, the mean does not reach the new score.
z-m-15-01.s.s2.prompt: Try 3 different values of x, the 6th game's score, so that the 6-game mean score is from 12 points to 13 points.
z-m-15-01.s.s2.hint.0: Write an expression for the total of the 6 games if the 6th game's score is x points.
z-m-15-01.s.s2.hint.1: Think backward: what must the total be for the mean to be 12 points? Then find the smallest value x can have.
z-m-15-01.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a whole number from 0 to 25 points.
z-m-15-01.s.s2.fail.c1: The score must be a whole number from 0 to 25 points.
z-m-15-01.s.s2.ok.c2: The 6-game mean is at least 12 points.
z-m-15-01.s.s2.fail.c2: The 6-game mean is short of 12 points.
z-m-15-01.s.s2.ok.c3: The 6-game mean is at most 13 points.
z-m-15-01.s.s2.fail.c3: The 6-game mean is greater than 13 points.
z-m-15-01.s.s2.explain: For the mean to be 12 points, the 6-game total must be 72 points, and for 13 points it must be 78 points. Since the total of the first 5 games is 55 points, x is a whole number from 17 to 23. All of 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23 are possible.
z-m-15-01.s.s3.prompt: A friend says, 'The mean now is 11 points, so if we just beat 12 points in the next game, the 6-game mean will be 12 points.' Use numbers to tell your friend why that is not so.
z-m-15-01.s.s3.hint.0: What value could you calculate to disprove your friend's claim with a single number?
z-m-15-01.s.s3.hint.1: First write down, 'What must the total be for the mean to be 12 points?'
z-m-15-01.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., Even if we score 12 points, ...
z-m-15-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check with numbers whether the mean changes all at once to match the new score?
z-m-15-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you look again to see whether the numbers you wrote came from a total or mean calculation?
z-m-15-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you point out where your friend went wrong (thinking the new score becomes the mean)?
z-m-15-01.s.s3.model.0: Even if we score 12 points, the 6-game total is 55+12=67 points, so the mean is about 11.2 points. For the mean to be 12 points, the total must be 72 points, so we need 17 points in the 6th game.
z-m-15-01.s.s3.model.1: The mean is a value made together by the first 5 games' scores and the new score, so one new score does not become the mean. For example, with 12 points the mean is about 11.2 points.
z-m-15-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: It did not find the score needed, but the disproof is enough.

z-m-15-02.title: Should a 0-page day be counted in the daily mean?
z-m-15-02.topic: Handling data values of 0 in a mean
z-m-15-02.goal: Learn that whether to include a data value of 0 depends on what the question asks the mean of, then find the wrong line in a solution and fix it to fit the condition.
z-m-15-02.material: Minseo wrote down the number of pages she read each day for 5 days, Monday through Friday. She read 20 pages on Monday, 0 pages on Tuesday, 15 pages on Wednesday, 0 pages on Thursday, and 25 pages on Friday. (0 pages means she did not read that day.) Minseo plans to give a presentation titled 'On average, how many pages a day did I read over these 5 days this week?' Below is Minseo's solution.
z-m-15-02.thinking.0: Finding the location of an error in a solution
z-m-15-02.thinking.1: Understanding that the answer changes depending on what the question asks about
z-m-15-02.thinking.2: Expressing the two means without misunderstanding
z-m-15-02.prereq.0: Experience knowing what the mean is and finding the mean of simple data (grades 5-6 level)
z-m-15-02.s.s1.prompt: In the solution that answers Minseo's presentation title 'On average, how many pages a day did I read over these 5 days this week?', choose one wrong line.
z-m-15-02.s.s1.hint.0: Reread the sentence to see which days the presentation title is about.
z-m-15-02.s.s1.hint.1: Find the mean once leaving out the 0-page days and once including them, and compare the two values.
z-m-15-02.s.s1.line.0: She read 20 pages on Mon, 0 on Tue, 15 on Wed, 0 on Thu, and 25 on Fri.
z-m-15-02.s.s1.line.1: A 0-page day is a day she did not read, so leave it out of the data.
z-m-15-02.s.s1.line.2: Adding the pages of the remaining days gives 20+15+25=60 pages.
z-m-15-02.s.s1.line.3: There are 3 remaining days, so 60÷3=20 pages.
z-m-15-02.s.s1.line.4: Therefore she read an average of 20 pages a day this week.
z-m-15-02.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is wrong. The title asks for the 'daily mean over 5 days,' so the 0-page days when she did not read must also be counted among the 5 days. The calculations in lines 3 and 4 are correct, but they are based on the data with those days left out, so the conclusion in line 5 does not match the question. Choosing line 2 or line 5 is correct. Counting all 5 days gives 60÷5=12 pages.
z-m-15-02.s.s2.prompt: Minseo changed the title to 'On the days I read, how many pages a day did I read on average?' How can we see the value 20 pages for this title?
z-m-15-02.s.s2.hint.0: Mark whether the new title is about all 5 days or only the days she read.
z-m-15-02.s.s2.hint.1: Write down which days were gathered to get 20 pages and which to get 12 pages.
z-m-15-02.s.s2.o.a: It is still a wrong value. A mean must always include the 0-page days.
z-m-15-02.s.s2.r.a: You generalized that 0 must 'always be included.' A mean can differ depending on which days it is about.
z-m-15-02.s.s2.o.b: Just use the larger of 12 pages and 20 pages.
z-m-15-02.s.s2.r.b: You tried to choose by the size of the value. You must choose according to which days the question asks about.
z-m-15-02.s.s2.o.c: It is a suitable value. Now the mean is taken over the 3 days she read.
z-m-15-02.s.s2.r.c: This judgment points out that when the subject of the question changes, the days to include in the data change too.
z-m-15-02.s.s2.o.d: Even if the title changes, 12 pages and 20 pages mean the same thing, so either value is fine.
z-m-15-02.s.s2.r.d: You missed that the two values answer different questions. Compare which days were gathered to find each mean.
z-m-15-02.s.s2.explain: If only the days she read (Mon, Wed, Fri) are used, 60 pages divided by 3 days gives 20 pages, which is suitable. If all 5 days are used, it is 12 pages. Even with the same data, when the subject of the question changes, what the mean refers to changes.
z-m-15-02.s.s3.prompt: You want to put both means in your presentation. Write how you would phrase each in a sentence so listeners do not misunderstand.
z-m-15-02.s.s3.hint.0: Try putting the words 'over which days' right before each value.
z-m-15-02.s.s3.hint.1: Check in which sentence the days she did not read disappear.
z-m-15-02.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., Over these 5 days this week, ...
z-m-15-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does your sentence show that the two values are about different days?
z-m-15-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is there any chance that listeners will misunderstand 12 pages and 20 pages as meaning the same thing?
z-m-15-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Is it clear which mean includes the 0-page days and which leaves them out?
z-m-15-02.s.s3.model.0: Over these 5 days this week I read 12 pages a day on average, and looking only at the 3 days I read, I read 20 pages a day on average.
z-m-15-02.s.s3.model.1: Over all of Mon to Fri it is 12 pages a day, and looking only at the days I read (Mon, Wed, Fri) it is 20 pages a day. I did not read on Tuesday and Thursday.
z-m-15-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: It is clearer because it states the days she did not read separately.

z-m-15-03.title: If the percentages on a graph add up to 101%, is it wrong?
z-m-15-03.topic: Writing percentages (rounding) and the total of 100%
z-m-15-03.goal: Explain that rounded percentages may not add up to 100%, and make such cases yourself to say what to watch out for when interpreting a graph.
z-m-15-03.material: 40 people were asked, 'Which one book do you want to read first?' and each chose only one of novel, science, or comics. A group wrote on a circle graph: novel 33%, science 33%, comics 35%, but the total is 101%. Each percentage is (the number of people who chose that item)÷40×100 rounded to the nearest whole number at the first decimal place. (Round up if the digit is 5 or more.)
z-m-15-03.thinking.0: Reasoning about possible causes when a result looks odd
z-m-15-03.thinking.1: Making a counterexample yourself to check
z-m-15-03.thinking.2: Explaining the limits of a way of displaying
z-m-15-03.prereq.0: Expressing a part of a whole as a percentage (grade 6 level)
z-m-15-03.prereq.1: Rounding to the first decimal place (grade 5 level)
z-m-15-03.s.s1.prompt: The total is 101%. What is the most suitable thing to say about this graph?
z-m-15-03.s.s1.hint.0: Work backward, one by one, to see how many of the 40 people 33%, 33%, and 35% correspond to.
z-m-15-03.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the numbers of people you found add up to 40, and write the exact percentages before rounding.
z-m-15-03.s.s1.o.a: Because each percentage was rounded, the total may not be 100%
z-m-15-03.s.s1.r.a: You noticed the condition that the written values are approximations. Checking with the real numbers of people makes your reasoning firmer.
z-m-15-03.s.s1.o.b: The percentages must always add up to exactly 100%, so a calculation must be wrong somewhere
z-m-15-03.s.s1.r.b: You treated the sum of approximate values as the same as the sum of exact values. Think separately about exact values and rounded values.
z-m-15-03.s.s1.o.c: A total of 101% means that 41 people answered
z-m-15-03.s.s1.r.c: You read the total of the percentages as a number of people. The whole is 40 people, so you need to look for a different reason the total goes over 100%.
z-m-15-03.s.s1.o.d: On a circle graph there is no need to check the total of the percentages
z-m-15-03.s.s1.r.d: You skipped checking the total at all. It is important to look for the reason when the total looks odd.
z-m-15-03.s.s1.explain: If each percentage is a rounded value, even when the exact values add up to 100%, the rounded values may add up to something different. In this data, if the numbers of people are 13, 13, and 14, the exact percentages are 32.5%, 32.5%, and 35%, and rounding gives 33%, 33%, and 35%. You cannot be sure without knowing the numbers of people, so it is good to check with the real numbers of people.
z-m-15-03.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 different cases, other than 13, 13, 14 above, in which the numbers of people who chose the three items, a, b, and c, add up to 40 but the rounded percentages do not add up to 100%. (Every number of people is at least 1.)
z-m-15-03.s.s2.hint.0: Pick a number of people and first find the exact percentage out of 40, before rounding.
z-m-15-03.s.s2.hint.1: Count how many percentages get rounded up (those where the first decimal digit is 5).
z-m-15-03.s.s2.var.a: Number of people who chose novel
z-m-15-03.s.s2.var.b: Number of people who chose science
z-m-15-03.s.s2.var.c: Number of people who chose comics
z-m-15-03.s.s2.ok.c1: Every number of people is a whole number that is at least 1.
z-m-15-03.s.s2.fail.c1: Every number of people must be a whole number that is at least 1.
z-m-15-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The three numbers of people do not add up to 40.
z-m-15-03.s.s2.ok.c3: The rounded percentages do not add up to 100%.
z-m-15-03.s.s2.fail.c3: The rounded percentages add up to 100%. It must be a case where they do not add up to 100%.
z-m-15-03.s.s2.ok.c4: It is a case different from the 13, 13, 14 shown at first.
z-m-15-03.s.s2.fail.c4: This is the 13, 13, 14 shown at first. Make a different case.
z-m-15-03.s.s2.explain: For example, with 5, 5, 30 people, the exact percentages are 12.5%, 12.5%, and 75%, and rounding gives 13%, 13%, and 75%, so the total is 101%. With 40 people, one person is 2.5%, so if two items have an odd number of people, .5 is rounded up twice and the total becomes 101%. If all are even, the total is 100%.
z-m-15-03.s.s3.prompt: A friend says, 'The total is 101%, so we can't use this graph. We have to do the survey again!' Write what you would tell your friend and what explanation you would add next to the graph.
z-m-15-03.s.s3.hint.0: First write in one sentence why your friend thinks it is wrong.
z-m-15-03.s.s3.hint.1: What could you add so that someone looking at the graph will not be surprised when they add up the percentages?
z-m-15-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you explain why the total can differ, in answer to the claim that the survey must be redone?
z-m-15-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you add an explanation so that people looking at the graph can understand even when the total is not 100%?
z-m-15-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you check that the numbers you wrote came from calculations with the numbers of people and percentages?
z-m-15-03.s.s3.model.0: Because each value was rounded, the total may not be 100%. Just write under the graph, 'The total may not be 100% because of rounding.'
z-m-15-03.s.s3.model.1: With 13, 13, and 14 people, the percentages are 32.5%, 32.5%, and 35%, but rounding to the first decimal place gives 33%, 33%, and 35%, so the total becomes 101%. We don't need to do the survey again.
z-m-15-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: It checks right away with the numbers of people, so it is the most convincing.

z-m-15-04.title: Is the bag with more red marbles the better one?
z-m-15-04.topic: Comparing chances (two cases with different totals)
z-m-15-04.goal: Decide what information you need to compare chances, revise the comparison when new information appears, and make an example showing that 'more' and 'more likely' are not the same.
z-m-15-04.material: There are bag 가 and bag 나. You close your eyes and take out one marble from each bag. The marbles differ only in color; their size and shape are the same. It is a game where you win if you take out a red marble. You take out a marble only once, and you do not put it back.
z-m-15-04.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
z-m-15-04.thinking.1: Revising a judgment with new information
z-m-15-04.prereq.0: Expressing the size of a part of a whole as a fraction
z-m-15-04.prereq.1: Comparing fractions with different denominators (grades 5-6 level)
z-m-15-04.s.s1.prompt: All we know now is that 'bag 가 has 3 red marbles and bag 나 has 5 red marbles.' What is the most suitable thing to say about which bag gives a higher chance of winning?
z-m-15-04.s.s1.hint.0: Imagine what happens if there are 100 other marbles even though there are 3 red ones.
z-m-15-04.s.s1.hint.1: Give one example of how the chance changes when the number of marbles of other colors changes, even with the same number of red marbles.
z-m-15-04.s.s1.o.a: Bag 나 is higher. It has 2 more red marbles.
z-m-15-04.s.s1.r.a: You compared only the number of red marbles. We cannot yet know what share of all the marbles are red.
z-m-15-04.s.s1.o.b: Bag 가 is higher. The fewer marbles a bag has, the easier it is to get a red one.
z-m-15-04.s.s1.r.b: You assumed the total number of marbles is small, but we do not have that information yet. It is a guess without grounds.
z-m-15-04.s.s1.o.c: We cannot compare unless we know the total number of marbles (or the number of marbles of other colors).
z-m-15-04.s.s1.r.c: You pointed out that the chance is decided by looking at the number of red marbles and the total number of marbles together.
z-m-15-04.s.s1.o.d: Red either comes out or does not, so the two chances are the same.
z-m-15-04.s.s1.r.d: You judged the chances to be the same just because there are two outcomes. The number of outcomes being the same does not make the chances the same.
z-m-15-04.s.s1.explain: The chance is figured by the share that red marbles take of all the marbles. Knowing only the number of red marbles, we do not know the total number of marbles, so we cannot say which is higher. In a case like this, it is suitable to first say 'what more we need to know.'
z-m-15-04.s.s2.prompt: There is new information. Bag 가 has 2 blue marbles and bag 나 has 4 blue marbles, and neither bag has marbles of any other color. Now, from which bag is the chance of winning higher?
z-m-15-04.s.s2.hint.0: First find the total number of marbles in each bag.
z-m-15-04.s.s2.hint.1: Write the two chances as fractions, make the denominators the same, and compare their sizes.
z-m-15-04.s.s2.o.a: Bag 가 is higher. The share of red marbles out of all marbles is larger.
z-m-15-04.s.s2.r.a: This judgment compares, as fractions, what part of the whole the red marbles are in the two bags.
z-m-15-04.s.s2.o.b: Bag 나 is higher. It has more red marbles, 5.
z-m-15-04.s.s2.r.b: Even with the new information, you compared only the number of red marbles. Check whether the total number of marbles has changed.
z-m-15-04.s.s2.o.c: The two bags are the same. In both bags there is 1 more red marble than blue marbles.
z-m-15-04.s.s2.r.c: You thought that if the difference between the red and blue counts is the same, the chances are the same. Even with the same difference, the totals differ, so the shares can differ.
z-m-15-04.s.s2.o.d: The totals of marbles differ, so we cannot compare even after calculating.
z-m-15-04.s.s2.r.d: You thought we cannot compare when the denominators differ. We can compare by making the denominators the same or by changing to decimals.
z-m-15-04.s.s2.explain: Bag 가 has 3 red out of 5 in all, which is 3/5 (0.6), and bag 나 has 5 red out of 9 in all, which is 5/9 (about 0.56). Making the denominator 45 gives 27/45 and 25/45, so bag 가 is a little higher. Even though bag 나 has more red marbles, the chance of winning is higher in bag 가.
z-m-15-04.s.s3.prompt: Make a case yourself in which the statement 'The bag with more red marbles always has a higher chance of winning' does not hold. Write the numbers of red marbles and total marbles in the two bags and explain why.
z-m-15-04.s.s3.hint.0: First, put a very small number of red marbles and a very small total in one bag.
z-m-15-04.s.s3.hint.1: Make the other bag have many red marbles but even more marbles of other colors, and compare the two chances by writing them as fractions.
z-m-15-04.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., Bag A has ... red marbles out of ... in all
z-m-15-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you make the bag with more red marbles have a lower chance of winning?
z-m-15-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you compare the chances of the two bags in the same way and show it with numbers?
z-m-15-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you explain in your example how 'there are more' differs from 'the chance is higher'?
z-m-15-04.s.s3.model.0: Bag 가 has 4 red and 1 blue, 5 marbles in all, and bag 나 has 6 red and 6 blue, 12 marbles in all. Bag 나 has more red marbles, but 가 has 4 out of 5 and 나 has 6 out of 12, so 가 is higher.
z-m-15-04.s.s3.model.1: Bag A has 3 red marbles out of 10 in all, so it is 3/10, and bag B has 1 red marble out of 1 in all, so it is sure to win. Even though A has more red marbles, B has the higher chance.
z-m-15-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: It is an extreme example, but it satisfies the condition.

z-m-15-05.title: Which graph is good for showing the same data?
z-m-15-05.topic: Choosing a graph to show data
z-m-15-05.goal: Compare how each kind of graph shows some things well and other things poorly, and choose a graph that fits the purpose, giving reasons.
z-m-15-05.thinking.0: Comparing and evaluating ways of showing data to fit a purpose
z-m-15-05.thinking.1: Telling apart what a graph shows from what it hides
z-m-15-05.thinking.2: Accepting that several choices can be valid
z-m-15-05.prereq.0: Can read line graphs and bar graphs (grade 4 level)
z-m-15-05.prereq.1: Knows that a circle graph or band graph shows the ratio of parts to a whole (grade 6 level)
z-m-15-05.s.s1.prompt: You want to show at a glance how the number of books borrowed from March to August changed (the flow of rising and falling). Which graph is most suitable?
z-m-15-05.s.s1.hint.0: Tell in a sentence whether what you want to show is 'how many each month' or 'how it changed as the months went by.'
z-m-15-05.s.s1.hint.1: Picture each graph in your head and compare whether the change from May to June stands out.
z-m-15-05.s.s1.r.a: This graph shows each month's share of the whole. It is not suitable for showing the flow of rising and falling as months pass.
z-m-15-05.s.s1.r.b: It is good for comparing sizes month by month. For showing a flow, a line graph may fit better.
z-m-15-05.s.s1.r.c: This graph divides the whole into one strip to show the shares. It is hard to show the direction of change over the months.
z-m-15-05.s.s1.r.d: You recalled that it is a graph that shows a quantity changing over time by the rising and falling of a line.
z-m-15-05.s.s1.explain: To show how values change as time passes, a line graph is the most direct. A bar graph can also compare month by month, but a line graph shows more clearly the line rising and falling as it connects.
z-m-15-05.s.s1.acc.0: A bar graph is also easy for comparing month by month, and the rising and falling can be read from the bar heights. However, the direction and size of change show more clearly at a glance in the slope of a line on a line graph.
z-m-15-05.s.s2.hint.0: First sort out whether a circle graph shows 'the number of books' or 'the share of the whole.'
z-m-15-05.s.s2.hint.1: Sort each choice into questions that a share can answer and questions that need order or the amount of change.
z-m-15-05.s.s2.o.a: About what percent of the whole 6 months the August borrowing was
z-m-15-05.s.s2.r.a: Reading the share a sector takes of the whole is the feature of a circle graph.
z-m-15-05.s.s2.o.b: By how many books borrowing fell between May and June
z-m-15-05.s.s2.o.c: The month with the most borrowing among the 6 months
z-m-15-05.s.s2.r.c: You can find this by looking for the biggest sector.
z-m-15-05.s.s2.o.d: Whether borrowing kept rising over the 6 months
z-m-15-05.s.s3.prompt: The friend who drew the circle graph says, 'Just looking at this graph, you can fully see the flow of borrowing going up.' Write your opinion to your friend, including both what a circle graph shows well and what it shows poorly.
z-m-15-05.s.s3.hint.0: First write one thing you can read from the sector sizes on a circle graph.
z-m-15-05.s.s3.hint.1: Then write one thing you can read from a line graph of the same data but that is hard to read from a circle graph.
z-m-15-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write both what can be known and what is hard to know from a circle graph?
z-m-15-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is there an example (such as August's share) that supports your opinion?
z-m-15-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you connect it to situations that need a line graph or another graph?
z-m-15-05.s.s3.model.0: A circle graph shows well the percentage each month takes of the whole. For example, August is the biggest sector. But it is hard to see the flow of going up and down as months pass, so to show the flow, a line graph is better.
z-m-15-05.s.s3.model.1: From the circle graph you can tell that August is the biggest, at about 23% of the whole. But the change of falling in June and rising again in July is hard to find out because there is no order or number of books.
z-m-15-05.s.s3.modelNote.1: It would be even better to add the hint that things could change if the number of books were also written.
z-m-15-05.material:
A school library surveyed the number of books borrowed each month from March to August.
March 350, April 380, May 420, June 300, July 410, August 560 (6-month total 2420)
We want to show this data in a graph. In the pie chart, we do not write the number of books or the total, only the size of the sectors and the month names, and the sectors are placed in order from the biggest.
z-m-15-05.s.s2.prompt: When drawn as a pie chart (without the number of books or the total, only the sector sizes and month names, with sectors placed from the biggest), choose everything you can tell right away from the graph alone.
z-m-15-05.s.s2.r.b: Sectors show only the share, and neither the number of books nor the total is written. You cannot tell from the graph alone how many books it decreased by.
z-m-15-05.s.s2.r.d: The sectors are placed from the biggest, so you cannot tell the order of the months. If you do not know the order, it is also hard to know the flow of increases and decreases.
z-m-15-05.s.s2.explain: In a pie chart, you can tell the shares and the biggest item from the sector sizes. August is 560÷2420, which is about 23%. But since the number of books is not written and the order of the months cannot be known, it is hard to tell from the pie chart alone how many books it decreased by or whether it increased over time.

z-m-15-06.title: The forecast said 70% chance of rain, but it did not rain
z-m-15-06.topic: Judging a forecast's chance by records
z-m-15-06.goal: Tell apart one day's result from records of many days, revise your judgment about chance and how sure you are each time the data grows, and design the records you need for judging.
z-m-15-06.material: A weather forecast said, 'Tomorrow's chance of rain is 70%.' Here, a chance of 70% means '70% of the way between no rain at all (0%) and rain for sure (100%).' We want to think about how trustworthy this forecast is by using records.
z-m-15-06.thinking.0: Revising judgment and certainty according to the amount of data
z-m-15-06.thinking.1: Telling apart one result from the records of many times
z-m-15-06.thinking.2: Deciding for yourself what data is needed for a judgment
z-m-15-06.prereq.0: Experience of expressing a chance as a number from 0 to 100%
z-m-15-06.prereq.1: The relation between percentages and fractions (grade 6 level)
z-m-15-06.s.s1.prompt: The data is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose how you would evaluate this forecast.
z-m-15-06.s.s1.hint.0: At each stage, find for yourself the number of rainy days divided by the total number of days, and compare it with 70%.
z-m-15-06.s.s1.hint.1: When the records grow, sort out which of your first judgments to keep and which to change.
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.0.info: The day after the forecast, it did not rain.
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.0.ask: How can you evaluate the forecast from this one day's result alone?
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.0.after: A chance of 70% means there is a 30% chance that it may not rain. From one day's result, it is hard to judge whether the forecast was right or wrong.
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.0.o.a: The forecast was wrong. It said 70% and it did not rain, so the forecast was not right.
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You read 70% as 'it rains for sure.' The 30% chance is the side where it does not rain.
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It is hard to say it was wrong from one day's result alone. The chance that it would not rain was also 30%.
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This judgment does not decide the chance from a single result, and also looks at the remaining chance.
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.0.o.c: The forecast was right. There was as much as a 30% chance of no rain, so the result matches the forecast.
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You decided it was 'right' because the result was no rain. From one result, it is hard to tell even whether it was right.
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.0.o.d: If the chance of rain is 70%, it rains for sure, so if it did not rain, the forecasting agency made a mistake.
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You treated 70% as the same as 100%. 70% is different from 'for sure.'
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.1.info: We gathered 10 days on which the same forecaster said 'a 70% chance of rain.' It rained on 7 days and did not rain on 3 days.
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.1.ask: Looking at this record, how would you evaluate this forecaster's 70% forecasts?
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.1.after: 7 days out of 10 is a record that matches 70% well. But 10 is a small number of days, so if you gather more, your certainty can become firmer. This record is a much more trustworthy clue than one result.
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The record matches 70% well, but 10 days is few, so we should gather more
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You looked at both that the record does not conflict with the forecast and that the amount of data is still small.
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The record does not conflict with the forecast, so we can trust this forecaster's 70%
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You raised your trust relying on the fact that the record matches the forecast. It would be even better to also be careful about the amount, 10 days.
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It did not rain on 3 days, so this forecaster's forecast was wrong
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You counted every day without rain as a 'wrong forecast.' 70% also means that it may not rain on about 3 days.
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.1.o.d: With 70%, it has to rain on all 10 days for the forecast to be right
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You read 70% as if it were 100%.
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.2.info: We gathered the first 10 days on which another forecaster said '70%,' and it rained on 2 days. After gathering 40 more days, there were 50 days in all, and it rained on 16 days in all.
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.2.ask: How would you evaluate this forecaster's 70% forecasts?
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.2.after: 16 days out of 50 is 32%. By the record of days on which 70% was forecast, it is very different from 70%. As the records grow, the explanation that the first result was a coincidence gets weaker, and your judgment changes toward the view that this forecaster's 70% is hard to trust as it stands.
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.2.o.a: 50 days is still few and it is only chance, so we can keep trusting the 70% forecast
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Even though the data grew to 50 days, you tried to hold on to your first belief. Look at the tendency the larger data shows.
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.2.o.b: No more records are needed, and we can decide that this forecaster's forecasts are already wrong
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You saw that 50 days of records are a clear clue, but you closed off the possibility of new data coming later.
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.2.o.c: We can't know each day's weather, so records gathered over many days are useless
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You threw away the clue that records of many days give. Even if you can't know one day, you can speak about the tendency over many days.
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.2.o.d: 16÷50 is 32%, which is very different from 70%, so it is hard to trust the 70% as it stands
z-m-15-06.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This judgment finds the ratio of rainy days in the record and compares it with the forecast chance.
z-m-15-06.s.s1.reflect: Each time you looked at the one day's result, the 10-day record, and the 50-day record, how did your judgment about 'Is this forecast trustworthy?' and how sure you were change? At which point did your certainty change the most?
z-m-15-06.s.s2.prompt: You want to find out whose 70% forecasts are more trustworthy among forecasters. Tell a friend what records to gather and how to organize them.
z-m-15-06.s.s2.hint.0: First think about what problem arises if you record only one day.
z-m-15-06.s.s2.hint.1: Write what names to give the table's cells so that you can count rainy days and non-rainy days separately.
z-m-15-06.s.s2.placeholder: e.g., Gather the days on which the same 70% was said ...
z-m-15-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you try to check with records of many days, not one day?
z-m-15-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you try to compare by gathering days with the same forecast chance?
z-m-15-06.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you write how to compare the ratio of rainy days with the forecast chance?
z-m-15-06.s.s2.model.0: Gather many days on which the same 70% was said, and organize in a table how many of them were rainy days. The more days, the more trustworthy, and compare whether the ratio of rainy days is close to 70%.
z-m-15-06.s.s2.model.1: Record about 50 days on which the forecast was 70%, count the rainy days and non-rainy days, find the ratio, and then compare it with 70%. Make a separate table for each forecaster.
z-m-15-06.s.s2.modelNote.1: Making separate tables for each forecaster is good.

z-m-15-07.title: Could more students get less than the average allowance?
z-m-15-07.topic: The difference between the mean and individual data
z-m-15-07.goal: Show with a counterexample that even with the same mean, most data values can be below the mean, and say when it is suitable to use the mean as a representative value.
z-m-15-07.material: The mean monthly allowance of a group of 5 people is 5천 원. Allowances are whole numbers in units of 1천 원, and all 5 people get at least 1천 원. If the allowance is written in units of '천 원,' the total of the 5 people's allowances is 25 (천 원) and the mean is 5 (천 원).
z-m-15-07.thinking.0: Testing a generalization with a counterexample
z-m-15-07.thinking.1: Making several data sets that satisfy a condition
z-m-15-07.thinking.2: Explaining the uses and limits of a representative value
z-m-15-07.prereq.0: Experience knowing what the mean is and finding the mean of simple data (grades 5-6 level)
z-m-15-07.prereq.1: Sums and size comparison of natural numbers
z-m-15-07.s.s1.prompt: To show that the thought 'The mean is 5천 원, so most of the 5 people must get at least 5천 원' can be wrong, what kind of case should you look for?
z-m-15-07.s.s1.hint.0: First write how many 천 원 you get when you add up all 5 people's allowances if the mean is 5천 원.
z-m-15-07.s.s1.hint.1: Think about what happens to the total of the other 4 people if one person gets far more than the mean.
z-m-15-07.s.s1.o.a: A case where all 5 people get exactly 5천 원 each
z-m-15-07.s.s1.r.a: If everyone gets 5천 원, all 5 people get at least 5천 원, so it does not conflict with that thought.
z-m-15-07.s.s1.o.b: A case where nobody gets less than 5천 원
z-m-15-07.s.s1.r.b: If nobody gets less than the mean, then everyone gets at least 5천 원, so it points the same way as that thought.
z-m-15-07.s.s1.o.c: A case where the total of the 5 people's allowances is more than 25 (천 원)
z-m-15-07.s.s1.r.c: If the total is not 25 (천 원), the mean is not 5천 원. You must keep the condition that the mean is 5천 원.
z-m-15-07.s.s1.o.d: A case where only 1 person gets at least 5천 원
z-m-15-07.s.s1.r.d: This judgment recalls a case where one person gets a lot and the others get less than the mean so that the total is 25 (천 원).
z-m-15-07.s.s1.explain: As long as the total is 25 (천 원), the mean is 5 (천 원). For example, with 3, 3, 3, 4, 12 (천 원), the total is 25 and the mean is 5, but the only person who gets at least 5천 원 is the 1 person who gets 12천 원. If even one such case exists, the thought 'The mean is 5천 원, so most get at least 5천 원' is not always right.
z-m-15-07.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 different sets of 5 allowances (in units of 천 원) in which the mean of the 5 people is 5천 원 and exactly 1 person gets at least 5천 원. (Ones with only the order changed count as the same case.)
z-m-15-07.s.s2.hint.0: Choose one person who gets at least 5천 원, and put each of the other 4 people at 4천 원 or less.
z-m-15-07.s.s2.hint.1: Once the total of the other 4 people is set, check that the one person's allowance is 25 minus that total.
z-m-15-07.s.s2.ok.c1: All are whole numbers that are at least 1.
z-m-15-07.s.s2.fail.c1: Every allowance must be a whole number that is at least 1천 원 (in units of 천 원).
z-m-15-07.s.s2.ok.c2: The total is 25 (천 원), so the mean is 5천 원.
z-m-15-07.s.s2.fail.c2: The total of the 5 people is not 25 (천 원).
z-m-15-07.s.s2.ok.c3: Exactly 1 person gets at least 5천 원.
z-m-15-07.s.s2.fail.c3: It is not exactly 1 person who gets at least 5천 원.
z-m-15-07.s.s2.explain: If the other 4 people all get 4천 원 or less, their total is at most 16 (천 원), so the 1 person must get at least 9천 원. Many cases are possible, such as 3, 3, 3, 4, 12 or 4, 4, 4, 4, 9. Even with the same mean, individual data can differ like this.
z-m-15-07.s.s3.prompt: Using the examples you made above, explain why the saying 'The mean is 5천 원, so the friends in this group probably get about 5천 원 each' may not be right, and also write when it is fine to use the mean as the representative value of this group.
z-m-15-07.s.s3.hint.0: Write exactly the numbers of one of the examples you made above.
z-m-15-07.s.s3.hint.1: On the other hand, think about how the mean would feel if all 5 people got between 4천 원 and 6천 원.
z-m-15-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you use the numbers of your example to show that 'most people get less than the mean'?
z-m-15-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you state at least one condition under which the mean can be used as a representative value?
z-m-15-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you tell apart its uses without declaring that the mean is useless?
z-m-15-07.s.s3.model.0: If one person gets a lot, the mean goes up, and the others get less than the mean. For example, with 3, 3, 3, 4, 12천 원, the mean is 5천 원 but 4 people get less than 5천 원. When people's allowances are similar to each other, it is fine to use the mean as the representative value.
z-m-15-07.s.s3.model.1: If one data value is much larger than the others, the mean is pulled toward that value and differs from most of the values. If the values are gathered close together, the mean is a suitable representative value.
z-m-15-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: It has no example numbers, but the reason and condition are clear.

z-m-15-08.title: Making the rules of a card game with different chances to win
z-m-15-08.goal: Check whether rules overlap, design your own game rules that fit the conditions, and write each player's chance of winning as a fraction, confirming that many designs are possible.
z-m-15-08.material: There are 20 cards, each with one number from 1 to 20 written on it. Shuffle all the cards, place them face down, and draw one. Each card is equally likely to be drawn. A and B play a game: A wins if a 'multiple of m' comes out, and B wins if a 'multiple of n' comes out. (m and n are different natural numbers from 2 to 20, and the players decide the values of m and n.)
z-m-15-08.thinking.2: Writing chances as fractions and comparing them
z-m-15-08.prereq.0: Knows multiples and can find multiples up to 20 (grade 5 level)
z-m-15-08.prereq.1: Expressing a part of a whole as a fraction (grades 5-6 level)
z-m-15-08.s.s1.prompt: First, we tried the rule that A wins if a multiple of 4 comes out and B wins if a multiple of 6 comes out. What is the first problem to solve in this rule?
z-m-15-08.s.s1.hint.0: Write out all the cards on which A wins and all the cards on which B wins, and place them side by side.
z-m-15-08.s.s1.hint.1: Look for any number that is in both lists.
z-m-15-08.s.s1.o.a: There are more multiples of 4 than of 6, so B cannot win at all
z-m-15-08.s.s1.r.a: The multiples of 6, which are 6, 12, and 18, are among the cards, so B can win too. List for yourself the cards each person can win with.
z-m-15-08.s.s1.o.b: If 12 comes out, both A and B win, so we cannot decide who won
z-m-15-08.s.s1.r.b: You pointed out that there is a card that fits both rules, so the rules overlap.
z-m-15-08.s.s1.o.c: There are 20 cards, so we cannot play a game with multiples
z-m-15-08.s.s1.r.c: You linked the number of cards to whether the game can be played. Even with 20 cards, a rule with multiples can be used.
z-m-15-08.s.s1.o.d: A's and B's chances of winning must be equal, so we must use the same number instead of 4 and 6
z-m-15-08.s.s1.r.d: If you use the same number, both players always win together. Being fair and not overlapping are different problems.
z-m-15-08.s.s1.explain: The multiples of 4 are the 5 cards 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, and the multiples of 6 are the 3 cards 6, 12, 18. 12 applies to both players, so if 12 comes out we cannot decide the winner. First we must check that there is no such overlap.
z-m-15-08.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 different rules (m, n) that satisfy all the following conditions. Conditions: ① No card makes both players win at the same time. ② A's chance of winning is higher than B's chance of winning. ③ B's chance of winning is also at least 2 out of 20.
z-m-15-08.s.s2.hint.0: List the cards that are multiples of m and the cards that are multiples of n, and check that there is no number in common.
z-m-15-08.s.s2.hint.1: First decide A's number of cards, then try n one by one so that B's number of cards is at least 2 and less than A's.
z-m-15-08.s.s2.var.m: The multiple m on which A wins
z-m-15-08.s.s2.var.n: The multiple n on which B wins
z-m-15-08.s.s2.ok.c1: m and n are different natural numbers from 2 to 20.
z-m-15-08.s.s2.fail.c1: m and n must be different natural numbers from 2 to 20.
z-m-15-08.s.s2.ok.c2: No card makes both players win at the same time.
z-m-15-08.s.s2.fail.c2: There is a common multiple of m and n within 1 to 20, so there is a card on which both players win at the same time.
z-m-15-08.s.s2.ok.c3: A has more cards on which A can win than B.
z-m-15-08.s.s2.fail.c3: A's chance of winning is not higher than B's.
z-m-15-08.s.s2.ok.c4: B has at least 2 cards on which B can win.
z-m-15-08.s.s2.fail.c4: B has fewer than 2 cards on which B can win.
z-m-15-08.s.s2.explain: For no card to overlap, the common multiples of m and n must be greater than 20, and you can count the number of cards as the quotient (rounded down) of 20÷m. For example, with (3, 7), A has the 6 cards 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 (6 out of 20) and B has the 2 cards 7, 14 (2 out of 20). Many rules are possible, such as (4, 7), (5, 6), (6, 10).
z-m-15-08.s.s3.prompt: Choose one of the rules you just made, write A's and B's chances of winning each as a fraction, and explain how you checked that no card makes both players win at the same time.
z-m-15-08.s.s3.hint.0: Write out all of A's cards and all of B's cards for the rule you chose.
z-m-15-08.s.s3.hint.1: Write in one sentence how you compared the two lists.
z-m-15-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write the two chances based on the same whole (20 cards)?
z-m-15-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say that you checked that there is no overlap by a method such as lists or common multiples?
z-m-15-08.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you check again that your rule satisfies all of conditions ①, ②, ③?
z-m-15-08.s.s3.model.0: My rule is that A wins on multiples of 3 and B wins on multiples of 7. A has the 6 cards 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, so it is 6 out of 20, and B has the 2 cards 7, 14, so it is 2 out of 20. The common multiples of 3 and 7 start from 21, so there is no overlapping card within 1 to 20.
z-m-15-08.s.s3.model.1: A has 5 cards that are multiples of 4, so it is 5/20, and B has 2 cards that are multiples of 7, so it is 2/20. I wrote out all the multiples of 4 and of 7 and there is no same card, so there is no case where both win at once.
z-m-15-08.s.s3.modelNote.1: It is a method that checks by writing out the lists directly.
